description: We are a collaborative team of students eager to build, test and experiment with our ideas. We focus on using real data to drive real-world impact.
summary:
Outpost Sol 4184 is a ten-day (~10 minutes in real-time) Mars game for children that opens in a browser. There is no account, no install, and no server. Accessibility is its greatest strength. The whole game is about 1.4 megabytes. The outpost, buttons, and icons are drawn in the page, and every sound is made in the browser as you play, so there are no audio files to download. A child on a slow connection can load it once and play.

A detailed, interactive tutorial is provided, built with children in mind. The game is short and easy to get started with. Each Martian day lasts one minute. Space pauses the clock, and any day can be started over. Large buttons, plain labels, a light or dark theme, mute, and reduced motion keep the screen welcoming and accessible. A clean, scrapbook style UI makes it look less like a control panel, and more like a storybook come alive. We aimed it at ages 9 and 10, and even younger children can follow it. The games brisk pace, and well-thought-out UI means that our game keeps even the most restless kids curious for more. Simple tasks unlock collectable science cards tied to real historical NASA events, so learning stays part of the play.
details:
Outpost Sol 4184

A ten-day Mars survival game for kids, built to load anywhere.

We are a team of three, and we made Outpost Sol 4184 because we think children should get to know space by playing in it. In the game you run a small outpost in Jezero Crater on Mars for ten days. Each day you finish simple tasks, keep the crew's power, air, water and health up, and get ready for a solar storm. Along the way you learn what astronauts actually need to stay alive on another planet.

The days are counted in sols, the Martian calendar. A sol is about 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds long, a little longer than an Earth day, and the game uses that real number. Our outpost is named for Sol 4184 for the same reason.

Anyone can open it

There is no login, no account and no download to install. You open a link and you are playing.

The game is a static web app, written in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, built with React and Vite. Nothing is served continuously from a server, so it costs almost nothing to host and works the same for a child in a city or a village. The sound effects and music are created inside the game itself, so there are no separate audio files to download. This matters because the places that most need free educational games often have the slowest connections.

No live data, on purpose

NASA publishes a lot of live space weather data, and we could have connected to it. We chose not to. Live API calls are slow and unreliable on weak connections, and one failed request can break a game for a child who has already waited a long time.

Instead, the solar storm in the game is a recorded sequence of events based on real NASA data from the May 2024 solar flare. It plays the same way every time, loads instantly, and still teaches something true.

Short, yet Sweet


The whole game is about 1.4 megabytes, pictures included. The outpost itself is drawn in the page, not stored as art files. Buttons, icons, and the Martian scene are code. Even the sound effects and the music are made in the browser while you play, so there are no audio files to download at all. The only pictures are the science-card photos, saved small. A child on a shared phone in a village can load it once and play. That small size is the point. A free educational game does little good if the download is the hard part. We want Outpost Sol 4184 to be a bright, easy thing to find on a slow connection: a beacon of play that still teaches something true.

A scrapbook, not a control panel

The game looks like a scrapbook, with bright colours, rounded shapes and big, clear task buttons. We wanted it to feel like a playbook a child already knows how to read. The look is friendly on purpose, and it should make a child want to click around.

Collecting cards

Finishing tasks earns science cards, fourteen in all (10 + 4 secret). Each card is tied to a real NASA source, so it is more than a sticker. After a child completes a task, the card explains what they just did and why it matters in real life. It might be how astronauts recycle water, why a wall of water can shield a crew from radiation, or how a rover keeps working in the dark. Wanting to finish the set keeps them playing, and each card teaches something along the way. Secret cards add to the mystery and cultivates the curiosity of the child.

Easy to start, a challenge by the end

We aimed the game at ages 9 and 10, and it can still work for children around seven. A first demo session walks the player through the basics step by step. In our design, children should have the rules figured out by day 2 or 3. After that the game gets harder at a normal pace, and by day 9 a player has to manage their resources carefully to get through. We kept the difficulty gentle on purpose, while also providing real consequences to actions, because the goal is for kids to understand the game, not to fail it.

Why we built it

We wanted to make a child curious about space with a game that is simple, good-looking and free for everyone. Outpost Sol 4184 is our attempt at that.
